questions.stem: German and Defeyter (2000) had children use an overturned box as a support so that a toy bear could reach a toy on a high shelf, after first seeing the box used as a container in one condition. What did they find about the youngest children?
options: Five-year-olds were not slowed by having seen the container use and were even faster than older children in that condition.
Five-year-olds were slowed the most by having seen the container use, more than the older children.
All age groups were equally slowed by having seen the container use, so age made no difference.
Five-year-olds could not solve the task at all, while older children solved it quickly after the container use.
questions.why: German and Defeyter (2000) found that 6- and 7-year-olds were slower after the container use was shown, while 5-year-olds were immune and were faster than the older children. The distractors reverse or erase this age contrast.

questions.stem: A child who has just watched a cup used to hold pencils cannot think of turning that same cup upside down to serve as a step stool. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Functional fixedness, being stuck on an object's usual function and failing to see another use.
Perseveration, repeating a previous response even after the situation has changed.
Mental set, applying a familiar solution method to a problem that needs a different approach.
Insight, suddenly seeing the whole solution after a period of impasse.
questions.why: Functional fixedness is being stuck on an object's usual function. The other terms name different problem-solving phenomena.

questions.stem: In the box task, German and Defeyter (2000) included a condition where children first saw the box used as a container and a condition where they did not. What did comparing these conditions allow them to separate?
options: The effect of having seen the box's usual container function from ordinary improvement in problem solving with age.
The effect of the toy bear's appearance from the effect of the shelf's height.
The effect of children's memory for the room from their motivation to please the experimenter.
The effect of adults' training from the effect of children's natural curiosity.
questions.why: Without the container demonstration children simply improved with age, so the contrast shows what the demonstration itself added: a slowing in the older children. The distractors name variables that the condition does not manipulate.

questions.stem: Leist and colleagues (2022) tested children and adults on memory for the order of verbal items and of spatial items while speech was played that they were to ignore. What did they find?
options: Speech impaired recall of verbal items but did not disrupt recall of spatial items in either age group.
Speech impaired recall of verbal and spatial items equally in both children and adults.
Speech impaired recall of spatial items more than verbal items, especially in adults.
Speech impaired recall only in adults, while children were unaffected for both kinds of items.
questions.why: Leist and colleagues (2022) found the irrelevant speech effect to be specific to verbal material; neither group was disrupted on the spatial task. The option claiming equal effects on verbal and spatial items is not what was found.

questions.stem: In studies of the irrelevant speech effect, speech made of different syllables is compared with one syllable repeated over and over. What is the first kind of speech called, and what is its effect?
options: Changing-state speech, which impairs serial recall more than steady-state speech does.
Steady-state speech, which impairs serial recall more than changing speech does.
Changing-state speech, which improves serial recall by helping rehearsal of the list.
Phonological speech, which impairs serial recall only when it is attended to.
questions.why: Changing-state speech (different syllables) impairs serial recall more than steady-state speech (one syllable repeated). The distractors swap the labels or invert the effect.

questions.stem: Why did Leist and colleagues (2022) test memory for spatial items as well as verbal items?
options: Because explanations based on order rehearsal or attention capture predict disruption for any item, while a verbal-specific account predicts disruption only for verbal items.
Because spatial items are easier to remember, which lets the speech effect be measured more precisely.
Because children are known to perform better on spatial than on verbal tasks at every age.
Because spatial items allow the speech to be left out of the task without changing anything else.
questions.why: Changing-state and attention-capture accounts predict spatial disruption too, whereas similarity-based interference with phonological representations predicts verbal-only disruption. Spatial items therefore separate these accounts; the distractors give reasons unrelated to the theories.

questions.stem: A student lists the items to buy in a notebook rather than trying to hold them in mind, to reduce the mental demands of the shopping trip. What is this action called?
options: Cognitive offloading, using actions such as writing things down to reduce the mental demands of a task.
Chunking, grouping separate items into larger meaningful chunks to hold more in mind.
Maintenance rehearsal, repeating items silently to keep them active in memory.
Elaborative encoding, linking new items to existing knowledge to deepen processing.
questions.why: Cognitive offloading is using actions like writing things down to reduce the mental demands of a task. The distractors are other memory strategies that keep the load in the mind.

questions.stem: Morrison and Richmond (2020) had people remember lists of letters of different lengths, sometimes with pen and paper available and sometimes with memory only. What did they find about offloading?
options: Offloading improved memory, especially at higher loads, and people offloaded more as the load grew.
Offloading improved memory equally at all loads, and people offloaded at the same rate regardless of load.
Offloading lowered memory at high loads, so people offloaded less as the load grew.
Offloading helped only at very small loads, and people offloaded most when the list was short.
questions.why: Morrison and Richmond (2020) found that offloading helped most at higher loads and that people offloaded more as the load grew. The distractors flip the load pattern.

questions.stem: A researcher expects that people with weaker working memory will write things down more often than people with stronger working memory. Which result did Morrison and Richmond (2020) obtain on this point?
options: Memory ability did not predict who offloaded or who benefited, suggesting offloading may help people across abilities.
People with weaker memory offloaded much more often and gained far more.
People with stronger memory offloaded more often because they could plan better how to use the notepad.
Offloading helped only the people with the strongest memory, since weaker people made errors when writing.
questions.why: Morrison and Richmond (2020) found no link between memory ability and offloading, and capacity did not predict the benefit, so offloading may help across abilities. The distractors assert a link that was not found.

questions.stem: According to one account, wrong answers on the bat-and-ball problem come from reasoners neglecting the phrase 'more than' and answering an easier question without noticing. What is this process called?
options: Unconscious attribute substitution, swapping an easier problem in for the harder one that was asked.
Confirmation bias, searching only for information that supports a belief already held.
Functional fixedness, being stuck on an object's usual function and missing a new use.
Anchoring, relying too heavily on the first number encountered when estimating.
questions.why: That account proposes unconscious attribute substitution, in which reasoners swap in an easier problem. The other labels are different biases.

questions.stem: Hoover and Healy (2019) tested people who gave the intuitive wrong answer to the bat-and-ball problem. What did they find about the phrase 'more than'?
options: Most incorrect reasoners could recall and recognize the phrase, so it was not simply overlooked, but they apparently did not use its meaning.
Most incorrect reasoners failed to notice the phrase at all, which confirms that it was overlooked.
Most incorrect reasoners understood the phrase fully but chose the wrong answer to be quick.
Most incorrect reasoners recalled the phrase only when told that their answer was wrong.
questions.why: Hoover and Healy (2019) found stronger evidence for a conscious error process: the phrase was processed but its meaning apparently was not used. The distractors say it was overlooked or fully understood.

questions.stem: Researchers compared the standard bat-and-ball problem with a control version that lacks the words 'more than'. What did this control version allow them to show?
options: That incorrect reasoners were less confident on the standard problem than on the control, suggesting they sensed something was off.
That incorrect reasoners were more confident on the standard problem than on the control, suggesting they felt sure.
That all reasoners solved the control correctly, which proves the standard version is unfair.
That the words 'more than' make the problem take longer to read but change nothing else.
questions.why: Incorrect reasoners were less confident on the standard problem than on the control without 'more than', which is called substitution sensitivity. The control isolates the effect of the phrase.

questions.stem: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) gave people life-or-death and financial choices with no default, a sure default, or a risky default. What did they find about defaults?
options: A risky default raised risk taking, while a sure default did not increase risk aversion.
A sure default raised risk aversion, while a risky default did not increase risk taking.
Both defaults pushed people equally toward the option that was preselected.
Defaults had no effect once people were given life-or-death wording.
questions.why: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) found that a risky default raised risk taking while a sure default did not raise risk aversion overall, so in some circumstances people can be nudged toward risk more easily than toward certainty. Framing and default had additive, independent effects.

questions.stem: In the research of Giuliani and colleagues (2023), people were asked afterward why they thought an option had been preselected. Which belief went with rejecting the default most often?
options: Thinking the default came from previous respondents or from chance.
Thinking the default was the most rational choice.
Thinking the default was a mistake in the survey.
Thinking the default was the safest and surest option.
questions.why: In this exploratory, after-the-choice question, Giuliani and colleagues (2023) found that people who thought the default came from previous respondents or chance tended to reject it most often, while those who saw it as the most rational choice followed it most. The other options describe beliefs that went with following or with nothing reported.

questions.stem: Chein and colleagues (2011) scanned people playing a driving game alone or watched by friends in another room. What did they find in adolescents when friends were watching?
options: Reward-related regions, the ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex, were more active, and this went with risky decisions.
Cognitive-control regions were much less active when friends watched than when alone, which explained the risky decisions.
Reward-related regions were less active, which explained why adolescents took fewer risks.
No brain region changed, so the extra risk taking was due to overt peer pressure.
questions.why: Chein and colleagues (2011) concluded the peer effect worked mainly through enhanced reward-circuit activity; cognitive-control regions did not change with peers, and friends were in another room, so it was not overt peer pressure.

questions.stem: Why did Chein and colleagues (2011) have participants play the driving game alone and also with friends watching from another room?
options: To compare friends watching without interacting during play against an alone baseline, so peer presence could be separated from overt peer pressure.
To separate the effect of practice from the effect of fatigue by repeating the game twice.
To separate the effect of friendship from the effect of the difficulty of the driving game.
To separate the effect of age by testing the same people at two different ages.
questions.why: Friends watching from another room, with no interaction during the task, is a peer context without overt pressure, so the alone baseline shows what the peer context adds. The distractors name variables the design does not isolate.
